passages.happening:
Hosea now tells his own story. The LORD says to him, ‘Go show love to your wife again, though she is loved by another and is an adulteress’ (verse 1). He is to love her as the LORD loves the Israelites, though they turn to other gods and offer raisin cakes to idols.

So Hosea buys her back for fifteen shekels of silver and a homer and a lethech of barley (verse 2). He tells her that she must live with him for many days. She is not to belong to another man, and he will do the same for her (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
This is a short report in the first person, like the sign acts of Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel, in which a prophet does something and then explains it. The word love comes four times in verse 1. It ties Hosea's love for his wife to the LORD's love for Israel, and it exposes the false loves of both. Raisin cakes were festive food, eaten at celebrations and apparently offered in the worship of other gods.

The price is part money and part goods. A shekel was a weight of silver, about 11 grams, not yet a coin. A homer was a large dry measure, often estimated at around 200 liters, though ancient measures are uncertain, and a lethech, named only here, was probably half a homer. Some interpreters reckon the whole came to about thirty shekels, the price of a slave in the law (Exodus 21:32), but the value of barley then is not known exactly. Paying partly in barley may mean Hosea did not have the full sum in silver. The text does not say why a payment was needed. She may have been in debt slavery, in another man's household, or bound to service at a shrine.

The many days of waiting are a time of restraint, in which she will not be with another man and Hosea will hold back from her as well. It is not rejection. It is a time for old attachments to be broken before the marriage is fully restored.
passages.later: The law set the price of a slave at thirty shekels of silver (Exodus 21:32), the sum some interpreters see behind Hosea's payment. Other prophets also acted out their message and then explained it, as Jeremiah did with a linen loincloth (Jeremiah 13:1-11) and Ezekiel with a brick drawn as a city under siege (Ezekiel 4:1-3).
passages.hard:
Is the woman in this chapter Gomer, and why must she wait?

The text says only your wife, or literally a woman, loved by another. Most interpreters, ancient and modern, take her to be Gomer, now gone after other men, and read the chapter as the sequel to chapter 1: the husband goes after the wife who left and restores her, just as God promises in chapter 2. Some scholars think she is a different woman and that this is a second sign, or the same marriage told again in Hosea's own words. The word again in verse 1 most naturally points to love renewed for someone already loved, which favors the first view. These notes do not settle it.

This is a prophetic sign of God's love for a nation that had left him. It is not a pattern for any marriage. It gives no warrant for any man to buy, confine, control, shame or harm a wife, and no one may use it to say that a wife must be kept or punished.

Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Hosea is told to love as the LORD loves Israel, though they turn to other gods. Ask what it means to you that God goes after people who have left him. And ask what loves in your own life compete with your love for God.

passages.t: Many days, and then the return
passages.happening:
Hosea explains the sign. ‘For the Israelites must live many days without king or prince, without sacrifice or sacred pillar, and without ephod or idol’ (verse 4).

‘Afterward, the people of Israel will return and seek the LORD their God and David their king. They will come trembling to the LORD and to His goodness in the last days’ (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Verse 4 lists what Israel will lose. King and prince are the political order. Sacrifice and the sacred pillar are the religious order: a sacred pillar was a standing stone set up at shrines, forbidden in the law but common in Israel's worship. The ephod was a priestly garment sometimes used to seek guidance from God, and the word rendered idol here means household images, perhaps of ancestors, also used to seek omens. The list mixes things that were allowed and things that were not. Exile would strip away both.

The words many days link the wife's waiting with Israel's time without a king. That came true in stages. After Jeroboam II the throne changed hands by murder again and again, and in 722 BC the kingdom ended when Assyria took Samaria and deported much of its people. The northern tribes never again had a king of their own.

David their king is striking in a word to the north. The northern tribes had broken from David's line two centuries earlier. Hosea's hope is that the divided people will come back not only to the LORD but to the royal line God chose. Some scholars think the phrase was added when the book was kept in Judah. Others point out that it fits 1:11, where Israel and Judah appoint one leader. They will come trembling, in awe, to the LORD and to his goodness.
passages.later: The northern tribes had cried that they had no share in David (1 Kings 12:16). Amos, Hosea's neighbor in time, also looked for the fallen house of David to be raised (Amos 9:11), and later prophets promised a king from David's line after the exile (Jeremiah 30:9; Ezekiel 34:23-24).
passages.asks: The many days without king or sacrifice were days of loss, and also days of waiting. Ask whether there has been a time when God took away what you leaned on, so that you would seek him. And ask what it would look like for you to come trembling to his goodness.
